headline_marked: Rescuers scour Nepal flood debris as [[death toll reaches 469]], nearly 1,000 missing
headline: Rescuers scour Nepal flood debris as death toll reaches 469, nearly 1,000 missing
summary: Flash floods and landslides, triggered by a glacier collapse, have devastated parts of Nepal and Tibet, leaving hundreds dead and thousands missing. Rescue operations are ongoing amid fears of further catastrophic flooding from a rising debris-dammed lake.
details: Rescue teams are digging through mud and debris in Nepalese towns devastated by flash floods, as hopes of finding survivors diminish. The confirmed death toll has risen to 469 people, with almost 1,000 more missing in Nepal and neighboring Tibet.

The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse on Wednesday morning, sending a massive torrent of rock, ice, mud, and debris through Himalayan river systems. The floods destroyed power stations, roads, and bridges along a route popular with trekkers and pilgrims, including the link between Kathmandu and Lhasa.

Among the missing, at least 540 are foreign nationals. Authorities in Nepal are using helicopters to search for survivors and drop emergency supplies, while emergency services, some with sniffer dogs, recover bodies swept into the plains.

Dibga Tamang, one of the last rescued from Rasuwa, described losing everyone. A new risk looms as a lake formed by debris blocking the Bhotekoshi River is rising and threatens to burst. China also expects a huge volume of water to flow into an already dammed lake.

Chinese authorities have mobilized an engineering team to conduct aerial surveys and 3D modeling of the barrier lake, but access is challenging due to isolated and steep cliffs. They are working to excavate a drainage channel and monitor the lake and weather.

Relatives worldwide are desperate for information about their missing loved ones, including dozens of Americans on a trek to Mount Kailash. US President Donald Trump has offered support to Nepal, noting the unprecedented destruction.

headline_marked: [[Yarn production drops to 30%]] as 660 textile mills face severe gas crisis
headline: Yarn production drops to 30% as 660 textile mills face severe gas crisis
summary: A severe gas crisis, primarily due to disruptions in LNG terminal operations, has crippled 660 textile mills across Bangladesh. Yarn production has plummeted to 30% of capacity, leading to partial shutdowns and substantial financial losses for many factories.
details: Six hundred and sixty textile mills across Bangladesh have been severely affected by a gas crisis since the third week of July, with yarn production plummeting to just 30% of capacity. Many factories are experiencing partial shutdowns, impacting a vital sector of the national economy.

Mosharraf Composite Textiles in Gazipur, for example, normally produces 170 tons of yarn daily but has seen production drop to 30% for over a month. The managing director reported a loss of approximately BDT 5 crore in the past month, leading to financial pressure in paying workers' wages.

The crisis intensified after an accidental fire shut down Exelerate Energy's LNG terminal on July 21, disrupting gas supply to industrial units. Although both Exelerate and Summit terminals partially or fully resumed operations by August 15, Exelerate's supply was again halted due to cargo issues, only restarting on August 22.

While some areas like Narsingdi have seen a slight improvement in gas pressure recently, many regions continue to suffer. Bhuiyan Textile & Calendar Mills in Narsingdi was closed for 22 consecutive days and can still only operate at night due to low daytime gas pressure.

The situation remains dire in Narayanganj, where MS Dyeing Printing & Finishing factory in Fatullah's BSCIC Industrial Park has been completely without gas since August 18. This has halted production, causing immense losses and disrupting the supply of fabric to garment sections.

Gazipur also presents a mixed picture; while some factories, like Asia Composite Mills, are now utilizing 70-75% of their yarn production capacity, many others still operate below 2 PSI gas pressure, limiting them to 30-35% capacity.

The Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA) informed the Commerce Ministry about the plight of these 660 mills, noting that 244 textile mills have already been closed since 2019. BTMA is currently assessing the situation and plans to propose initiatives to revive the affected factories.

BTMA Vice President Abul Kalam stated that his own factory in Narayanganj's Sonargaon has seen production drop to 40% due to the gas shortage. He highlighted that the prolonged crisis has financially weakened textile mills and raised concerns among foreign buyers, though he expressed hope for an improving gas situation.
